paper_title: CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-agnostic animation compression with a learned entropy model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Skeletal motion is stored as every joint's transform at every frame, yet most of it is implied by the body rather than by what the motion is about. Compression is one way to ask what a motion must still say once the body is known, and a production codec must answer it for any skeleton with a stated error bound. Our earlier codec, CurveCodec, matched the mean error of ACL, the production library of modern game engines, with a learned prior over sparse anchors, but not ACL's worst case, and it counted its payload as floats rather than bits. Here we ask where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies and which part of a codec a learned model should take over. Measurements give three answers. At production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each quantized curve from its own past, the second from choosing per joint, in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples not to code. On the gaps such an encoder leaves, a nearest-neighbour oracle over millions of training samples is no better than linear interpolation, and no learned in-betweener we tried paid for itself. What a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals the codec must send. CurveCodec 2 codes every sub-track as a curve in the log map, quantized in closed loop and thinned to rate-distortion-selected keys, with residuals entropy-coded under a small learned model whose integer inference is bit-exact across platforms. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL's own worst case per joint within a stated tolerance, or ACL's mean error per clip. On a held-out test side of 4,472 clips from 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37x ACL's bytes at ACL's default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract and 0.22x at 0.1 cm under the mean contract, decodes on one CPU core, and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training. Project page: https://rubbly.cn/publications/curvecodec/

sections.content: 2 Mingyi Shi, Huancheng Lin, Xuelin Chen, and Taku Komura morphology and its dynamics, determines most of how each joint gets from one place to the next. Compressing these data matters in production, where animation libraries face strict memory and streaming budgets, and in motion research, where corpora reach hundreds of hours and model should spend its capacity on the decisions rather than on kinematics the body already implies. codec is one way to probe this separation: what it must still send under stated error bound is at least what the body did not predict. This is our motivation, not claim the bit counts prove. If the body is only prior, the representation should not be tied to one body: production codec must serve arbitrary skeletons and motion without retraining, and it must bound its error, because single visible pop on one joint is defect regardless of how small the average error is. ACL [Frechette 2023] is the industry standard. It folds the subtracks that do not move, reduces the range of the rest per clip and per segment, and quantizes each joint with one of fixed set of bit widths under per-joint error threshold. It decodes pose in microseconds, but it models neither time nor the statistics of its own symbols. Learned motion encoders [Guo et al. 2024; Ling et al. 2020; Yao et al. 2024] take the opposite trade: their latent priors couple the representation to training skeleton and domain, and they do not reach production precision. Our previous work, CurveCodec [Shi et al. 2026], placed the learned prior on the smallest skeleton-independent unit of motion, the local joint curve, and reconstructed each curve from sparse anchors with shared transformer. It reached three times ACLs ratio at matched mean error, but its worst case exceeded ACLs, its payload was counted in floating-point values rather than entropycoded bits, and its decoder needed GPU rather than CPU core. This paper asks different question: where is the redundancy in skeletal motion, and which part of codec should learned model take over? We answer it by measurement, treating the codec as an instrument: under an explicit error contract and an exact bit count, every candidate structure of motion either pays or does not. We dissect ACL stage by stage and test every place where learned component could enter. Three findings shape the result. First, ACLs ratio comes almost entirely from folding and from range reduction with variable bit widths. Its widths are nearly tight for independent samples, so an entropy coder on top of ACLs own symbols would gain little; substantially smaller stream needs its own quantizer, one whose integers remain predictable in time. Second, at production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each curve from its own past, and the next from choosing, per joint and in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples to omit. Leaving sample out is by far the cheapest way to spend error, and its share of the stream grows as the precision loosens, until the two are comparable at the loosest precision we use. Third, on the gaps such an encoder leaves, interpolation has little left to find. nearest-neighbour oracle with millions of training samples as memory, which clearly beats cubic interpolation on random gaps, is no better than linear interpolation on the gaps the encoder actually leaves, and the learned in-betweeners we placed inside the codec did not pay. On our data, the in-betweener at the core of CurveCodec has little left to learn; what network does learn is the distribution of the residuals that the codec still has to send. These findings lead to CurveCodec 2. Every animated sub-track is coded as curve: rotations in the log map, which removes the precision floor of ACLs dropped quaternion component; quantization step and key set chosen in closed loop against the object-space error of the whole subtree; and prediction residuals coded with rANS under small learned model of the curves own past, causal transformer or, in the worst-case configuration, an MLP. The model sees no joint identity, so the codec is skeleton-agnostic, and its integer inference is bit-exact on ARM and x86. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACLs own worst case per joint, within stated tolerance, or ACLs mean error per clip. clip that fails is re-encoded with margin or stored as ACLs stream, and every number we report includes this fallback. On corpus of 906 hours from 33 datasets with held-out test side, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37 ACLs bytes at ACLs default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract, and 0.22 at 0.1 cm under either contract; against ACL with its default keyframe stripping the ratios are slightly larger and the picture is the same. It decodes on CPU, typically clip in fraction of second on one core, but only whole clips: it is storage and distribution format decoded at load time, not replacement for ACLs constant-time sampling. Our contributions are: quantitative anatomy of motion redundancy, measuring where production codecs bits go and which structure codec exploited in our hands: temporal predictability and, increasingly as the precision loosens, per-joint sample sparsity did; interpolation from the decoded neighbourhood, crossjoint structure, and transforms under worst-case criterion did not. CurveCodec 2, closed-loop, skeleton-agnostic rate distortion codec under two explicit error contracts, with stated fallback for the clips that fail. learned entropy model in the role where network pays: small, causal, and bit-exact across platforms, it models the distribution of the residuals the codec must send, the one place where, in our measurements, network consistently earns its cost. corpus-scale benchmark against ACL, with audits of ACLs configuration and of our own contracts, and samecore speed.

sections.title:
2.1 Hand-engineered Animation Compression
Before deep learning, animation compression removed temporal
redundancy, inter-joint redundancy, and perceptually insignificant
sections.content: CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-Agnostic Animation Compression with Learned Entropy Model 3 detail while keeping the motion faithful. Mesh compression began with static connectivity and geometry [Karni and Gotsman 2000; Rossignac 1999]; animated meshes were then compressed through their vertex trajectories, by principal components [Alexa and Müller 2000] or space-time prediction [Ibarria and Rossignac 2003]. Arikan [2006] moved the problem to skeletal motion: joint angles were converted into virtual marker trajectories, fitted with cubic Bézier curves, and projected into clustered PCA subspaces. Later work exploited low-dimensional structure with segment-level PCA and spline interpolation [Liu and McMillan 2006], quadratic Bézier break-and-fit curves [Khan 2016], wavelet coefficient selection [Beaudoin et al. 2007; Lee and Lasenby 2008], and wavelets guided by perception [Firouzmanesh et al. 2011]; others indexed repeated motion patterns across database [Gu et al. 2009; Lin et al. 2011]. ACL [Frechette 2023] is the production standard. It prioritizes per-track processing and constant-time random access over compression ratio, and Sec. 5.1 quantifies where its bits go. Our keys relate to keyframe extraction [Halit and Capin 2011; Lim and Thalmann 2001] and curve simplification [Barkowsky et al. 2000], which choose samples from local error or saliency criterion. CurveCodec 2 instead chooses them by ratedistortion optimization against the object-space error of the whole subtree, and Sec. 5.2 shows that this closed loop, not the key representation itself, carries the gain. Unlike transform codecs, which we find lose to sparse keys under worst-case criterion, CurveCodec 2 keeps the time domain and predicts each sample from its own past.

sections.title:
2.2 Learned Motion Representations and Codecs
Motion manifolds and deep motion representations show that valid
character motion occupies a much smaller space than raw joint rota-
tions [Holden et al. 2016, 2015]. VAE-style priors support character
control, action-conditioned synthesis, and pose estimation [Ling
et al. 2020; Petrovich et al. 2021; Rempe et al. 2021]; tokenizers
with vector or residual quantization compress motion into discrete
codes [Guo et al. 2024; Yao et al. 2024]; phase-based models orga-
nize motion by periodic timing [Shi et al. 2023; Starke et al. 2022];
and Learned Motion Matching [Holden et al. 2020] amortizes an
animation database into networks. Cross-skeleton methods learn
representations for retargeting [Aberman et al. 2020; Lee et al. 2023;
Villegas et al. 2018]. These representations target synthesis, con-
trol, or transfer at pose level, not a decodable bitstream at a stated
precision; SAME [Lee et al. 2023] in particular learns an embed-
ding shared across skeletons, which is a different goal from ours
rather than a competing codec. The learned encoders measured
in CurveCodec [Shi et al. 2026] under the shell metric reconstruct
with errors two orders of magnitude above the 0.01 cm of a produc-
tion codec, and the residual-VQ tokenizer we built has a precision
floor of about 1.3 % of a track’s RMS (Sec. 5.4); we do not extend
these bounds to methods we did not measure. Implicit neural repre-
sentations fit signals with coordinate networks [Chen et al. 2021;
Dupont et al. 2021; Park et al. 2019; Sitzmann et al. 2020; Tancik
et al. 2020], and NeMF [He et al. 2022] applies the idea to kinematic
motion. We find the same fidelity floor for per-window neural fields.
CurveCodec [Shi et al. 2026] is our direct predecessor. It made the
learned prior skeleton-agnostic by working on single sub-tracks,

3.2 Two-Stage Compression Pipeline
As in CurveCodec, we view compression as two stages (Fig. 2). The
first, deterministic preprocessing shared by ACL and CurveCodec 2,
drops the scale sub-tracks that ACL’s raw convention reserves and
folds every sub-track that does not move within 𝑝 into a single
default or constant value. Production skeletons contain many such
joints: on our corpus, dropping scale reduces ACL’s raw 647 GB to
453 GB, and at 𝑝 = 0.01 cm folding leaves only 53 % of the rotation
and 3.6 % of the translation sub-tracks animated. CurveCodec 2
applies ACL’s folding rule unchanged, so both codecs start the
second stage from the same animated sub-tracks.

4.4 Prediction and Learned Entropy Coding

sections.title:
5.1 ACL’s Bit Budget
Fig. 4a follows ACL’s stages on the curated set. Two stages do the
work: folding sub-tracks that do not move (2.84×, from 191 to 68
bits per joint-sample) and range reduction with variable bit widths
(3.74×, to 18.1 bits); the 4× spread of ACL’s ratio across datasets
comes from folding. Of the remaining bytes, 81 % are animated
rotations and 13.5 % per-segment range metadata, a share that grows
to 24 % at 0.1 cm on the test side because it does not shrink with
the precision. Fig. 4b asks what a lossless back end could add. The
zeroth-order entropy of ACL’s quantized samples is 97.7 % of the
bits it spends, so its widths are nearly tight for independent samples;
first and second differences reach 83.8 and 81.1 %, and real context
coders 0.80×. These bounds hold for the models we tried, up to
second-order temporal context; little is left because range reduction
stretches every 16 samples to fill their integer range.
sections.content: Consequence. substantially smaller stream needs its own quantizer. Ours is close to ACL in zeroth-order entropy (0.92 to 1.07), but its first differences cost 0.57 to 0.62 ACLs bits against 0.84 for ACLs own symbols: the gain appears once time is modelled.

sections.title: 5.2 Samples Predicted and Samples Not Coded
sections.content: Temporal predictability. Predicting each integer from its own past reduces the log-map stream by 39 to 55 % against its zeroth-order cost. The best predictor depends on the joint and capture: second differences beat first differences by 18 % at the root but only 4 to 7 % at depth six and below, where noise at the scale of the step dominates, and an adaptive (NLMS) predictor wins on 37 to 44 % of the curves, which motivates per-curve choice. Per-joint sparsity. Not every sample needs coding. Under the max gate the encoder keeps 87 % of the roots samples but only 57 % at depth six and below at 0.01 cm, and 51 against 22 % at 0.1 cm (Fig. 5a; five development clips, an earlier version of the encoder); the root keeps the most because its error reaches every descendant. ACL can only strip whole frames whose every joint is linearly interpolable, 0.38 % of the curated frames at 0.01 cm. Where keys pay, the gain comes from the closed loop: removing keys by local per-curve error bound saves only 0 to 0.6 %. The price of bit. At the margin, keys are the cheapest way to spend error. Fig. 5c compares the distortion the iso-mean encoder adds per bit it saves at 0.1 cm: growing step by one grid unit costs 0.17 step units, dead zone 0.31, and removing an RD-selected key about 0.03. This says which move to prefer, not how much each move contributes in total, which depends on how many cheap moves the precision leaves: on held-out data, removing keys from the final codec costs 8 % at 0.01 cm and 69 % at 1 cm, where it matches prediction (Sec. 6.5). Codecs that code every sample lose accordingly: dyadic hierarchical codec with learned in-betweener matches ours where keys keep 83 % of the samples (1.01) but needs 1.55 to 1.78 the bytes where they keep 7 to 15 %. Consequence. Prediction is the largest saving at 𝑝 0.1 cm and the choice of which samples to omit the second, with share that grows as 𝑝 loosens. The encoder needs both, with steps and keys competing for one budget. Fig. 4. Where ACLs bits go on the curated set. (a) Bits per joint-sample after each ACL stage: almost all of the 17.7 ratio comes from folding subtracks that do not move (2.84) and from the two-level range reduction with variable bit widths (3.74). (b) Entropy of ACLs own quantized symbols relative to the bits ACL spends, for zerothto second-order models: an entropy coder with these models on top of ACL saves at most 16 to 20 %, so substantially smaller stream needs different quantizer, not just better back end. the active columns, and the decoder reconstructs each integer before the next features are computed. For the max-gate codec we use 22 K-parameter MLP (36 128 128 9) over the same features, 4 cheaper to decode. Bit-exact inference. Encoder and decoder must compute identical probabilities. We export the network to fixed point: 16-bit weights with power-of-two scales, 64-bit integer accumulators, integer layer normalization, and lookup tables for softmax, sigmoid, and exponential. The residual stream is clipped to 228, which bounds every operand downstream: linear-layer products stay below 243 and their sums over at most 256 terms below 253, so even float64 matrix library adds exact integers [Ballé et al. 2019]; the attention logits and the layer-norm variance are accumulated in 64-bit integers within the bounds given in Appendix H. The guarantee is that every probability and every decoded integer is identical on any platform. The float reconstruction (dequantization, interpolation, Exp) runs on those integers and reproduced x86 results bit for bit on an ARM machine in our tests, but it is deterministic rather than exact by construction (Appendix H). Training. The model minimizes the code length of Eq. (8) on residual streams of our training split (886 h, 41.2 symbols), on 40 windows with 128 context positions and 384 scored ones, with AdamW [Loshchilov and Hutter 2019] and one-cycle schedule, in about 1.5 hours on one RTX 4090. Supplementary Appendix summarizes the bitstream layout; the reference decoder defines the details it leaves out.

sections.title:
5.4 Where a Network Pays
Tab. 1 summarizes every role we gave a network. Dense learned rep-
resentations have a precision floor: a residual-VQ tokenizer cannot
represent a track below about 1.3 % of its RMS and a meta-learned
neural field not below 1.6 to 4.8 % of the window’s amplitude, while
the contract asks for 0.01 to 0.1 %, so both degenerate into scalar
residual codecs. In a lifting-wavelet codec of ours, learning the trans-
form changed the size by ±1 % while learning its entropy model
saved 7 to 12 %; learned image codecs report a similar division of
gains [Ballé et al. 2018; Minnen et al. 2018], an analogy rather than
evidence for our numbers. Over a hand-designed context coder, the
MLP entropy model saves 3 to 7 % on mocap and 13 % on game
assets. It does not predict the next residual’s value (𝑅2 ≤ 0.02) but
its distribution, from a slowly varying per-curve regime: the resid-
ual’s scale relative to the step, periodicity, and whether a curve is
held, linear, or noisy. Eight positions of context give 60 to 70 % of
the gain. Supplementary Sec. F reports that cross-joint structure
(mirroring, pose-space PCA, interpolation context) and transforms
under a worst-case contract did not pay on our data.
sections.content: Consequence. The network belongs in the probability model, where it models distribution the codec must send anyway, and it can be small, causal, and local.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: No random access. CurveCodec 2 decodes whole clips: the coder, predictors, and model step are sequential in time, so single pose cannot be read in constant time, which ACL does in about half microsecond, and full clip takes 38 to 168 ACLs decompression time on one core, still far faster than real time (Sec. 6.6). This is inherent to the design, not matter of optimization: ACL is stateless and keeps the clip compressed in memory, decompressing only the poses runtimes evaluation pass needs, whereas CurveCodec 2 is storage and distribution format decoded at load time, and reencoding into ACL adds second lossy stage. Encoding is 4.8 to 12 slower than ACL and runs offline, in parallel over clips. Contracts relative to ACL. Both contracts take their targets from ACLs result on the same clip, so the encoder needs ACLs statistics and inherits its misses at loose precision; the max gate holds ACLs worst case only within 5 % tolerance, and errors are bounded at the sample times, not between them. standalone contract in terms of 𝑝 costs 4 to 6 % of the bytes on test subset but was not run at corpus scale. At loose precision the max-gate encoder does not un-fold tracks (Sec. 6.3); the fix is not part of the benchmarked codec. Not validated as representation. We motivated the codec by the hope that what it must send is closer to the motions decisions than to the body, but we test it only as codec. Neither the stream nor the entropy model is evaluated on generative or recognition task, and the findings that interpolation, cross-joint structure, and transforms did not pay hold for the estimators, data, and precisions we tried, each with one architecture and training run; they do not prove that no such model can do better. Whether the codec can serve learned motion model is future work.
